network.overall_strategy: Use two parallel feeder modules and keep the known bottlenecks explicit. Module A makes the carbon skeleton as alpha-ketoglutarate from glyoxylate plus pyruvate, then closes to glutamate by four literature-backed options: FeS reductive amination, Ni/H2 reductive amination, glycine transamination, or Bucherer-Bergs-type hydantoin hydrolysis. Module B keeps the contested aldehyde/nitrile family explicit by making the C4 bottleneck intermediate 3-cyanopropanal from acrolein, then forming the glutamate aminonitrile and hydrolyzing it. Pyroglutamate is retained as a reversible surface reservoir because glutamate cyclizes readily under warm dry conditions. The network is intentionally modular rather than one-pot, because the literature does not yet provide an integrated uncontested glutamate synthesis; where sequences mix environments, they should be read as handoffs between settings rather than as a single vessel. The purely thermodynamic one-step CO2/NH4+/H2 route is omitted from the core graph because kinetic support is much weaker than for the modular routes.

reactions.name: Fe2+-promoted alpha-ketoglutarate formation from glyoxylate and pyruvate

conditions.other: Anoxic, near-neutral to mildly alkaline vent fluids; graph-level net-balanced compression of aldol, dehydration, and reduction through omitted hydroxyketoglutarate and oxopentenedioate intermediates.

reactions.mechanism: Aldol addition of glyoxylate to pyruvate followed by dehydration and reduction to alpha-ketoglutarate.
reactions.reasoning: Fe2+ in warm water converts pyruvate and glyoxylate into alpha-ketoglutarate through hydroxyketoglutarate and oxopentenedioate chemistry (Muchowska et al., 2019). H2 is written as the net reductant so the node is mass-balanced and consistent with H2-rich vent fluids; related H2-driven reductive aldol chemistry was also demonstrated in a low-temperature metal-catalyzed setting (Kaur et al., 2024). This is a coarse-grained but chemically motivated hydrothermal alpha-KG supply step, and the literature still lacks one-pot closure from this module to glutamate.

reactions.name: Phosphate-buffered alpha-ketoglutarate formation from glyoxylate and pyruvate

conditions.other: Near-neutral phosphate-rich pool; graph uses H2 as a net reductant for the experimentally observed aldol, dehydration, and redox sequence.

reactions.mechanism: Phosphate-catalyzed aldol chemistry between glyoxylate and pyruvate followed by dehydration and net reduction to alpha-ketoglutarate.
reactions.reasoning: Stubbs et al. (2020) showed that metal-free phosphate-buffered glyoxylate/pyruvate networks produce alpha-ketoglutarate, making this the best-supported surface alpha-KG supply module. The graph writes H2 as a net reductant to close the condensed sequence, while the experimental system uses internal glyoxylate-mediated redox rather than proven free-H2 uptake; this is therefore a deliberate coarse-graining of a real literature pathway. The step remains a bottleneck because alpha-KG yield is modest and integrated conversion onward to glutamate has not been demonstrated one-pot.

reactions.name: Fresh FeS reductive amination of alpha-ketoglutarate

conditions.other: Anoxic alkaline interface near the NH4+ pKa; H2 represents net reducing equivalents delivered at the sulfide surface.

reactions.mechanism: Imine formation between alpha-ketoglutarate and ammonia followed by mineral-assisted hydrogenation to glutamate.
reactions.reasoning: Fresh FeS and related reduced iron sulfides promote nonenzymatic reductive amination of alpha-ketoacids, and glutamate formation from alpha-KG is among the stronger reported cases (Huber & Wachtershauser, 2003; Kitadai et al., 2019). H2 is written as the net source of reducing equivalents while FeS supplies the reactive surface and electron-transfer chemistry. Mayer & Moran (2022) showed that alpha-KG is intrinsically one of the slowest ketoacids to aminate, so this remains a key kinetic bottleneck despite strong mineral support.

reactions.name: Ni/H2 reductive amination of alpha-ketoglutarate

conditions.pressure: 1 atm to mildly elevated local H2 fugacity
conditions.other: pH about 8; low-temperature mineral pores or shallow geothermal settings; competing alpha-hydroxyglutarate formation expected.

reactions.mechanism: Ammonia adds to alpha-ketoglutarate to form an imine that is hydrogenated on Ni-bearing mineral or meteoritic surfaces.
reactions.reasoning: Ni/SiO2-Al2O3, Pd/C, and meteoritic NiFe catalyze H2-dependent reduction of alpha-KG to glutamate under mild conditions; Kaur et al. (2024) reported amino acid formation but also substantial hydroxy-acid competition. This node uses the balanced net stoichiometry for reductive amination and preserves the competing hydroxy-acid channel only in the reasoning, not as a separate product node. Mayer & Moran (2022) again argues that alpha-KG amination is intrinsically sluggish, so catalyst choice is crucial.

reactions.name: Glycine transamination of alpha-ketoglutarate

conditions.other: Concentrated glycine and phosphate-rich solution or mineral interface; no metal catalyst required.

reactions.mechanism: Nonenzymatic transamination transfers the amino group from glycine to alpha-ketoglutarate, regenerating glyoxylate.
reactions.reasoning: Stubbs et al. (2020) showed that alpha-ketoacid analogue networks permit nonenzymatic transamination using glycine, making this the most biology-congruent non-reductive closure from alpha-KG to glutamate. The step is mass-balanced as glycine donates nitrogen while becoming glyoxylate. Direct glutamate-specific yields were not separately optimized in that study, so this edge is plausible and literature-guided but less directly quantified than FeS- or Ni-driven reductive amination.

reactions.name: Bucherer-Bergs-type glutamate hydantoin formation

conditions.other: Cyanide-bearing, ammonia-bearing pool; Bucherer-Bergs-like condensation; literature often uses DAP as activator or ammonia donor.

reactions.mechanism: Cyanide and ammonia capture the alpha-ketoacid and close to a hydantoin ring.
reactions.reasoning: Pulletikurti et al. (2022) showed that alpha-ketoacids, including alpha-KG, can be converted to hydantoins in cyanide-containing chemistry, providing an explicit bridge between cyanide routes and metabolism-like alpha-ketoacid routes. The literature commonly uses diamidophosphate as the ammonia donor or activator; here NH3 is written as the minimal formal nitrogen source to keep the node compact and balanced. This route is experimentally strong for hydantoin formation, but its cyanide dependence remains debated.

reactions.name: Hydrolysis of glutamate hydantoin

conditions.other: Hydrolysis step; formal stoichiometry consumes 2 H2O and is typically incomplete.

reactions.mechanism: Hydrolytic ring opening of the hydantoin followed by decarboxylative release of ammonia and carbon dioxide to give glutamate.
reactions.reasoning: Hydrolysis of the glutamate hydantoin releases glutamate with CO2 and NH3 as byproducts, matching the Bucherer-Bergs closure reported by Pulletikurti et al. (2022). Experimentally the hydrolysis was incomplete and glutamate yield lagged far behind hydantoin formation, so this is an experimentally supported but inefficient finishing step. The formal stoichiometry in the graph corresponds to uptake of two waters.

reactions.name: HCN addition to acrolein

conditions.other: Aqueous post-discharge or pool chemistry; mildly basic conditions favor cyanide addition.

reactions.mechanism: Michael addition of cyanide to the activated enal gives the C4 nitrile aldehyde 3-cyanopropanal.
reactions.reasoning: Acrolein was identified or proposed in Miller-type discharge mixtures and suggested as a glutamate precursor by Van Trump & Miller (1972). Michael addition of HCN to acrolein gives the required C4 nitrile aldehyde, 3-cyanopropanal, which directly addresses the known C4-precursor bottleneck. The organic step is credible, but explicit prebiotic closure from spark-made acrolein to glutamate remains unmeasured, so this edge is partly speculative.

reactions.name: Strecker-type aminonitrile formation from 3-cyanopropanal

conditions.other: Net-balanced compression of cyanohydrin formation and ammonia capture to the aminonitrile.

reactions.mechanism: Cyanide first forms a cyanohydrin at the aldehyde, and ammonia then gives the alpha-aminonitrile.
reactions.reasoning: Patel et al. (2015) explicitly placed 3-cyanopropanal on the cyanosulfidic route to the glutamate or glutamine aminonitrile through cyanohydrin capture followed by ammonia addition. This node compresses those two experimentally motivated substeps into a single balanced Strecker-like transformation. The need for sequential reagent delivery, UV exposure, and sulfide-rich local settings remains a major caveat (Patel et al., 2015; Ranjan et al., 2018).

reactions.name: Hydrolysis of glutamate aminonitrile

conditions.other: Prolonged hydrolysis; formal stoichiometry consumes 4 H2O and releases 2 NH3.

reactions.mechanism: Sequential nitrile hydration to amides and then carboxylates yields free glutamate.
reactions.reasoning: Hydrolysis of the glutamate aminonitrile to free glutamate is the canonical Strecker closure and is consistent with trace glutamate in Miller extracts and with glutamate release from cyanide-derived precursor inventories (Johnson et al., 2008; Parker et al., 2011; Ruiz-Bermejo et al., 2013). The graph writes only the net stoichiometry; mechanistically the reaction proceeds stepwise through amide stages. This branch is literature-supported in family terms but low-yield for glutamate specifically.

reactions.name: Cyclization of glutamate to pyroglutamate

conditions.other: Favored by mild acidity and dry-down; faster above about 60 C.

reactions.mechanism: Intramolecular lactamization of glutamate with water loss gives the five-membered pyroglutamate ring.
reactions.reasoning: Glutamate readily cyclizes to pyroglutamate under drying, acidic, or warm conditions; this is a major sink emphasized by thermal and hydrothermal studies (Wu et al., 2010; Weiss et al., 2018; Lee et al., 2014). Because early surface pools undergo wet-dry cycling, excluding this sink would overstate free-glutamate persistence. Pyroglutamate is therefore treated as a reservoir, not just a loss product.

reactions.name: Hydrolytic reopening of pyroglutamate

conditions.other: Rewetting or hydrolytic reopening of the lactam; slower than cyclization under mild conditions.

reactions.mechanism: Hydrolysis of the lactam reopens pyroglutamate to free glutamate.
reactions.reasoning: Pyroglutamate can reopen to glutamate on hydrolysis, and meteoritic analyses treat pyroglutamate as an acid-labile glutamate precursor (Pizzarello & Cooper, 2001). Under mild prebiotic conditions this back-reaction is slower and less certain than cyclization, so the edge is plausible but partly speculative as a robust environmental source. It is included because the literature indicates pyroglutamate can store glutamate equivalents rather than destroy them irreversibly.

pathways.name: Hydrothermal Fe2+ supply plus FeS amination
pathways.description: Hydrothermal production of alpha-ketoglutarate followed by FeS-mediated reductive amination in the same broad vent-like setting.

pathways.name: Hydrothermal Fe2+ supply plus Ni/H2 amination
pathways.description: Hydrothermal alpha-ketoglutarate formation followed by low-temperature Ni-catalyzed H2 amination in a later shallow mineral setting.

pathways.name: Hydrothermal alpha-KG with glycine transamination
pathways.description: Hydrothermal carbon-skeleton formation followed by later surface transamination with glycine; modular rather than one-pot.

pathways.name: Hydrothermal alpha-KG with hydantoin bridge
pathways.description: Hydrothermal alpha-ketoglutarate is exported to a cyanide-bearing surface pool, trapped as hydantoin, and hydrolyzed to glutamate.

pathways.name: Surface phosphate alpha-KG plus FeS amination
pathways.description: Surface phosphate chemistry generates alpha-ketoglutarate, which is later aminated on reduced iron sulfides under hydrothermal conditions.

pathways.name: Surface phosphate alpha-KG plus Ni/H2 amination
pathways.description: Surface alpha-ketoglutarate supply followed by mild Ni/H2 reductive amination in an H2-rich mineral setting.

pathways.name: Surface phosphate alpha-KG plus glycine transamination
pathways.description: Entirely low-temperature pool chemistry: phosphate-mediated alpha-ketoglutarate generation followed by glycine transamination.

pathways.name: Surface phosphate alpha-KG with hydantoin bridge
pathways.description: Surface alpha-ketoglutarate is converted by cyanide and ammonia chemistry to glutamate hydantoin and then hydrolyzed.

pathways.name: Acrolein-Strecker nitrile route
pathways.description: Atmospheric or spark-derived acrolein is trapped by HCN, converted to the glutamate aminonitrile, and then hydrolyzed.

pathways.name: Acrolein-Strecker route with pyroglutamate reservoir
pathways.description: The nitrile route first makes glutamate, which then partially cyclizes during warm dry phases and is later re-opened from the pyroglutamate reservoir.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Best-supported branch. alpha-KG formation from glyoxylate plus pyruvate and FeS-mediated reductive amination are both literature-backed in hydrothermal aqueous settings. The main weakness is that rxn_001 is a compressed net step that hides known intermediates and assigns an external H2 input that is not explicit in all cited versions.
suggestions: Expand rxn_001 to the literature sequence through hydroxyketoglutarate and oxopentenedioate, or explicitly justify the H2-dependent shorthand.
Specify moderate hydrothermal conditions and fresh FeS or Fe(OH)2 with pH near the NH4+/NH3 crossover to avoid overextending the vent scenario.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Chemically plausible and literature-backed as a modular sequence, but it joins a hydrothermal alpha-KG-forming step to a distinct Ni/H2 surface reduction step without an explicit transfer or concentration mechanism. The Ni/H2 amination is supported experimentally, yet surface implementation likely needs a confined H2-rich setting and competing hydroxy-acid formation should be acknowledged.
suggestions: Add an explicit hydrothermal-to-surface handoff or concentration step for alpha-KG.
State the Ni-bearing catalyst and localized H2-rich conditions more explicitly, and include the competing alpha-hydroxyglutarate or hydroxy-acid channel.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Coherent alpha-KG branch, but glycine-to-glutamate transamination is less directly established for alpha-KG under prebiotic conditions than FeS or Ni/H2 amination. The hydrothermal-to-surface handoff is acceptable only if transport and concentration are made explicit.
suggestions: Provide direct experimental conditions showing alpha-KG plus glycine giving glutamate and glyoxylate under the stated surface setting.
Consider adding a catalyst or cofactor analogue only if it is explicitly justified for the same environment, or model equilibrium-driving removal of glyoxylate.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: The hydantoin bridge is literature-aligned and sensibly keeps cyanide chemistry explicit, but rxn_006 is under-specified relative to the reported alpha-KG hydantoin chemistry, and rxn_007 should be written as hydantoin plus 2 H2O giving glutamate plus NH3 plus CO2. Hydrolysis to glutamate is experimentally incomplete rather than a clean quantitative closure.
suggestions: Add the missing reagent context for the hydantoin step, such as the activating or carbamylating source used in the literature, or justify the NH3 and HCN-only shorthand.
Correct rxn_007 stoichiometry to include 2 H2O and note that hydrolysis is only partial under reported conditions.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Good modular route using phosphate-mediated alpha-KG production followed by a well-supported FeS amination. Weak points are the shorthand rxn_002 stoichiometry and role of H2, plus the unmodeled transfer from phosphate-rich surface chemistry to FeS-bearing hydrothermal or sedimentary conditions.
suggestions: Replace or justify external H2 in rxn_002 and, if possible, spell out the known phosphate-network intermediates.
Add an explicit handoff to the FeS setting and constrain temperature to the moderate range used in reductive amination studies.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: One of the better surface-only modules. Both steps are chemically plausible, but rxn_002 compresses a more complex phosphate network and rxn_004 requires a fairly specific Ni-bearing, H2-rich setting; the literature also reports amino-acid and hydroxy-acid mixtures rather than exclusively glutamate.
suggestions: Expand rxn_002 into the literature-supported phosphate sequence or clarify that it is a net summary rather than a single step.
Specify the Ni mineral or supported catalyst, H2 availability, pH, and competing hydroxy-acid branch for rxn_004.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Conceptually coherent, but both steps are the less secure versions of the alpha-KG module. Phosphate-generated alpha-KG is supported, yet glycine transamination to glutamate needs clearer direct experimental anchoring and may require conditions not fully compatible with the phosphate stage.
suggestions: Provide direct literature support for alpha-KG plus glycine giving glutamate under the same surface conditions used after phosphate alpha-KG formation.
If a catalyst is needed for transamination, state it explicitly and address any incompatibility with phosphate-rich conditions.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: All-surface hydantoin route fits the modular strategy, but it inherits the compressed phosphate alpha-KG step and the low-conversion hydantoin hydrolysis problem. rxn_007 needs an extra H2O coefficient, and the actual literature route benefits from more explicit reagent and temperature staging.
suggestions: Clarify whether rxn_006 is meant to follow the published alpha-KG hydantoin chemistry and include the necessary activating or carbamylating context.
Correct rxn_007 to hydantoin plus 2 H2O giving glutamate plus NH3 plus CO2, and note that hydrolysis is incomplete under reported conditions.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Strecker logic is correct and the network appropriately keeps 3-cyanopropanal explicit, but the weakest edge is still rxn_008: acrolein to 3-cyanopropanal is chemically plausible yet only proposed, not convincingly demonstrated under prebiotic conditions. rxn_010 must be corrected to aminonitrile plus 4 H2O giving glutamate plus 2 NH3.
suggestions: Supplement or replace the acrolein branch with a more explicitly evidenced 3-cyanopropanal supply route if stronger support is desired.
Correct rxn_010 stoichiometry and specify the hydrolysis regime needed for a dinitrile to reach glutamate.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Including pyroglutamate is a literature-aligned strength because glutamate readily cyclizes, but the reverse step is drawn too simply: pyroglutamate reopening is possible yet usually harsher or slower than generic surface hydration. This branch captures a realistic sink or reservoir, but not an easy reversible loop.
suggestions: Keep pyroglutamate as a side reservoir, but specify distinct warm or dry cyclization conditions for rxn_011 and harsher aqueous hydrolysis conditions for rxn_012.
Correct rxn_010 to aminonitrile plus 4 H2O giving glutamate plus 2 NH3 and make clear that the nitrile route still hinges on the weakly supported acrolein to 3-cyanopropanal step.

evaluation.network_feedback: Connected, modular, and strongly aligned with the literature review. The network reaches glutamate by several plausible branches and correctly keeps alpha-KG, 3-cyanopropanal, and pyroglutamate explicit as bottlenecks or reservoirs. Network validity is high: there are no isolated subgraphs and the RDKit check reports no unbalanced reactions, although rxn_007 should be written with 2 H2O and rxn_010 with 4 H2O and 2 NH3. The strongest chemistry is the alpha-KG module, especially the hydrothermal Fe2+ plus FeS closure and the alternative Ni/H2 closure, which is consistent with the separate experimental literature from Muchowska or Stubbs, Huber and Wachtershauser or Kitadai, and Kaur. The hydantoin bridge also aligns well with Pulletikurti in spirit, though its reagents and hydrolysis limitations are under-specified here. Main remaining weaknesses are that rxn_001 and rxn_002 are compressed net transformations, rxn_008 is only weakly supported in a prebiotic context, and rxn_012 overstates how easily pyroglutamate reopens. Overall this is a good, literature-aware network, but it is not approved at the network threshold because several key edges remain shorthand or contested rather than a fully closed, environment-specific end-to-end sequence.
